title: Ways to start a fire: matches, lighter, metal match, battery, lens, flint and steel, friction

answer: Start the fire from the upwind side, to protect the fragile heat source.
Modern fire-starters are the quickest and easiest. Primitive methods can be improvised from the natural environment, but generally take more skill and time.

Matches: keep them waterproof, in a waterproof container, with a striker pad. After the head ignites, hold it pointing down at an angle so the flame climbs the matchstick, protect the flame from the wind, then hold the match near the bottom edge of the tinder. Do not push it into or tightly against the tinder: that smothers the flame.

Lighter: light the tinder the same way as with a match. In extreme cold the fuel can freeze up and not work: warm the lighter with body heat. If a liquid-fuel lighter runs out of fuel, its sparking mechanism can still be used like a metal match.

Metal match (made of the same material as cigarette-lighter flints): reliable in wet or dry conditions and in cold or hot weather. Place the bottom end of the stick firmly on or near the edge of the tinder, hold the edge of the striker at a 90-degree angle to the stick, and drive the striker down the stick with even pressure to throw sparks into the tinder. Stop the stroke before the striker disturbs the tinder or the sparks.
The back of a fixed-blade knife or a similar tool can serve as the striker for a metal match.

Battery from a vehicle or electronic equipment: connect an insulated wire to the positive post and another to the negative post, then touch the two free ends to a third piece of uninsulated wire. The short gives a spark or a superheated piece of metal that ignites the tinder. Fine-grade steel wool stretched between the two posts also heats up and produces a coal.

Lens from binoculars, a camera, a telescopic sight or a magnifying glass: only on bright, sunny days. Angle the lens to concentrate the sun's rays on the tinder, hold it over the same spot until the tinder begins to smolder, then gently blow or fan it into flame.

Flint and steel: strike a flint or other hard, sharp-edged rock with a piece of carbon steel. Stainless steel does not produce a good spark. When the tinder catches a spark, blow on it. Charred cloth is the preferred tinder.

Fire plow (friction): cut a straight groove in a softwood base and plow the blunt tip of a hardwood shaft up and down the groove, with more pressure on each stroke, until the friction ignites the wood particles.

Bow and drill (friction): simple in concept, but it needs significant preparation: a socket, a drill, a fireboard, a fire pan and a bow. Prepare the base, brace, tinder and kindling first. The drill is spun in the fireboard until a coal forms. The coal is closed lightly inside a bird's nest of very dry, fine tinder and blown on with long steady breaths until it bursts into flame.
Hand drill (friction): needs less preparation than the bow and drill, but is more difficult for some to operate. Pressure is applied to the top of the drill while the hands rotate it.
Primitive methods take more energy, patience and skill than modern fire-starters. People who practice them beforehand are much more likely to succeed.
warnings: Before lighting, clear the ground of fallen leaves, vegetation and duff, exposing soil at least 3 feet (1 meter) across, to prevent the fire from spreading along the ground.
Protect a lit match from the wind. Each match that fizzles out or is blown out is one fewer fire you can start.
Battery method: keep any open flame away from the battery. Certain batteries produce explosive hydrogen gases that could cause injury.
Do not pour highly flammable liquids on an existing fire. Even a smoldering fire can make them explode and cause serious burns.
When you are finished with a fire, put it out. An adequate amount of water puts out a fire that is not burning petroleum-based fuel; dirt or sand works well on petroleum-based fires.
Before leaving the area, make sure the ground under where the fire was built is cool to the touch.

quotes.text: Fires are started from the upwind side to protect the fragile fire-starting heat source. Several different techniques can be used to ignite tinder.

While primitive methods allow for greater flexibility since they can be improvised from the natural environment, they generally require more skill and time to execute. Modern methods are the quickest and easiest method to start a fire, but they can only start a certain number of fires until the resource is exhausted.

Ensure that these matches are waterproof, stored in a waterproof container, and have a striker pad. Isolated persons take intentional precautionary measures to protect lit matches from wind. Each match that fizzles out or is blown out by wind represents one fewer fire that the isolated person can start in the future.

Once the match head is ignited, it is held with the match head pointing down at an angle so the flame can begin to climb the matchstick and gain strength. It is critical that the flame is protected from the wind during this step. Once the initial flame gains strength, the match is held near the bottom edge of tinder to ignite it. Caution is used to avoid snuffing out the small match flame by placing it into or tightly against the tinder and smothering it. Lighters are used to ignite tinder similarly to matches.

Under extreme cold temperatures, lighter fuel can freeze up and not function. In such situations, body heat can be used to warm the lighter. If the fuel runs out of a liquid-lighter, the sparking mechanism can be used similar to a metal match.
Metal matches are reliable and not effected by wet or dry conditionals, cold or hot weather, evaporation or age, and do not malfunction.
Most commercial metal matches include a striker to do this, but the back of a fixed-blade knife, tang end of a folding knife blade, or other similar tool can also accomplish the task just as well.
Metal matches are made of the same type material used for flints in commercial cigarette lighters.

Holding the striker at a 90-degree angle against the stick typically produces the best sparks. Good sparks from a metal match burn hot, fast, and can compensate for some moisture in tinder. The following are instructions for using a metal match to start a fire:
Grasping the stick at the top, place the bottom end of the stick firmly on or near the edge of tinder setting on a secure base.
Hold the edge of the striker at a 90-degree angle to the top of the stick.
Drive the striker downward with evenly applied pressure through the strike to near the bottom of the stick. This will throw a substantial amount of sparks into the tinder of done correctly.
Terminate the downward strike prior to the striker disturbing the tinder or recently thrown sparks to avoid snuffing them out.

Batteries found in vehicles, aircraft, or electronic equipment can be used as a field-expedient firestarter. Two insulated wires are required in addition to the battery to utilize this method. Once wire is connected to the positive post of the battery and the other wire is connected to the negative post. The two ends are touched to a third piece of uninsulated wire.

A short in the wire will result and cause a spark or a superheated piece of metal to ignite the tinder. Similarly, fine-grade steel wool can be stretched between the two posts of the battery causing the steel wool to heat up and produce a coal.
Isolated persons need to be careful to keep any open flame away from the battery. Certain batteries produce explosive hydrogen gases that could result in injury.
Use this method only on bright, sunny days. The lens can come from binoculars, a camera, telescopic sights, or magnifying glasses. Angle the lens to concentrate the sun's rays on the tinder.
Hold the lens over the same spot until the tinder begins to smolder. Gently blow or fan the tinder into a flame.
The direct-spark method is the easiest primitive method to use. Strike a flint or other hard, sharp-edged rock with a piece of carbon steel. Stainless steel does not produce a good spark.

This method requires a loose-jointed wrist and practice. When the tinder catches a spark, blow on it. The spark will spread and burst into flames. Charred cloth is the preferred tinder for this method.

To use this method, cut a straight groove in a softwood base and plow the blunt tip of a hardwood shaft up and down the groove. The plowing action of the shaft pushes out small particles of wood fibers. As more pressure is applied on each stroke, the friction ignites the wood particles.

The bow and drill method is simple in concept but requires significant preparation initially. Isolated persons will need to improvise several parts including a socket, drill, fireboard, fire pan and bow from materials located in their nearby surroundings.
The base, brace, tinder, and kindling are prepared prior to operating a bow and drill.
When in use, the bowstring is twisted around the drill once to rotate it as it spins or drills into the fireboard producing the friction needed to create a coal.
Tinder used for a bow and drill fire must be very dry, fine fibrous material made into the shape of a birds nest.
The bird nest is then lightly closed around the coal and lightly waved through the air or lightly blown on with long steady breaths to heat the coal and surrounding tinder.
The amount of smoke coming from the inside of the bird’s nest will continue to increase until it bursts into flame, at which time it is placed on the base where kindling is added.
A hand drill is a simpler method than the bow and drill in that it requires less preparation. However, its operation is more difficult for some.
To operate a hand drill, pressure is applied to the top of the drill while rotating the hands to spin it in short bursts equal to the length of the hands.
They can be time consuming to construct and require greater energy, patience, and skill to learn in comparison to modern firestarters.
Personnel that practice these skills before isolation are much more likely to be successful in constructing and using primitive fire-starters.
Highly flammable liquids should not be poured on an existing fire. Even a smoldering fire can cause liquids to explode and cause serious burns.
Clear the ground of fallen leaves, vegetation, and duff; expose 3 feet (1 meter) in diameter of soil at a minimum to prevent the fire from spreading along the ground.

When completed with a fire it is extinguished using materials such as water, entrenching tools, dirt or sand, and sturdy sticks that are prepared in advance. A fire is extinguished by removing one of the fire triangle elements. Fires with nonpetroleum-based fuel can be extinguished with an adequate amount of water. Large pieces of burning wood can be separated and the coals can be raked off with a tree branch. Some burning fuel can be broken apart and scattered over bare soils. Dirt or sand works well to extinguish petroleum-based fires.
When leaving an area after having a fire, ensure that the ground under where the fire was built is cool to the touch.
